newsitem.title: CANADA: Cash-rich Methanex could fund big project.
newsitem.headline: Cash-rich Methanex could fund big project.

text.p: Methanex Corp, the world's biggest methanol producer, said Thursday it was cash rich and would have the means to fund a major project or distribution to shareholders although no decision has been made.

Chief executive Pierre Choquette told a conference call that Methanex had US$450 million in cash at the end of the second quarter and undrawn credit facilities of about US$385 million despite repurchasing US$57.8 million in shares.
The company generated cash flow from operations of US$109.5 million in the second quarter. "That's a lot of cash generation," Choquette said.
He said Methanex was in the same position as late last year when management told its board of directors that the company had "cash beyond our strategic needs."
"The preferred uses (for the cash) would be to grow the business and look at strategic opportunities," he said.

The current cash hoard would enable Methanex to complete its 14 million-share buyback program, finish construction of a third methanol plant in Chile, handle its normal capital spending and undertake either a US$300 million "strategic project" or a US$200 million distribution without violating internal guidelines on leverage, Choquette said.
But he gave no hint of any imminent plans to pay a distribution to shareholders or embark on a major project.
Methanex has previously said it was seeking to build new production hub and was looking at sites in Asia. The company also sought unsuccessfully earlier this year to buy a methanol plant in Trinidad.

Choquette said Methanex was not interested in buying a high-cost 500,000-tonne methanol plant owned by Imperial Chemical Industries Plc rumored to be for sale. He said Methanex was more interested in supplying methanol to the British company.

Methanol is a chemical used in a variety of applications including paints, resins, building materials, formaldehyde and additives for cleaner burning gasoline. Demand has traditionally been closely linked to the economic cycle.
Methanex earlier reported second-quarter earnings of US$64.7 million, up from US$10.6 million a year earlier.

Choquette said the company was pleased with the results and described sales volume growth as very strong. The company has seen a growth rate of about 17 percent while it estimates the market as a whole is growing about five percent.
Sales have "continued to be a little bit beyond our expectations," Choquette said, adding that supply disruptions at other producers created some shortages.

That situation forced Methanex to scramble somewhat to keep up with demand and this has resulted in some costs to be higher than expected, notably for purchasing natural gas -- the raw material for methanol -- and shipping. Although this put it above its cost targets, it was not a long-term worry, Choquette said.

Choquette said the company was holding talks with New Zealand gas producers about potentially extending supply contracts for its plant there which expire starting in 2003. He said Methanex was encouraged but there were no results yet.
Methanex also plans to expand testing of more environmentally friendly diesel-methanol fuel blends.

In addition it has signed an accord with Ballard Power Systems Inc to work on developing a methanol supply infrastructure, Choquette said. Ballard is working with Daimler-Benz AG to develop an emission-free electric car that could run on methanol.
